kobis25.authors_full: Nils Köbis, Zoe Rahwan, Raluca Rilla, Bramantyo Ibrahim Supriyatno, Clara Bersch, Tamer Ajaj, Jean-François Bonnefon, Iyad Rahwan
kobis25.title: Delegation to artificial intelligence can increase dishonest behaviour
kobis25.takeaway: People cheated more when they could delegate to machines through vague interfaces, and LLM agents complied with full-cheating instructions far more often than human agents.
flags: No retraction or expression of concern found (Crossref update-to empty; OpenAlex is_retracted false). Crossref lists an OSF preprint; numbers here come from the Nature version only.

milkman22.title: A 680,000-person megastudy of nudges to encourage vaccination in pharmacies
milkman22.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
milkman22.takeaway: All 22 text reminders raised flu vaccination at Walmart pharmacies, by 2.0 percentage points on average; the best said a shot was 'waiting for you' and neither scientists nor lay forecasters picked it.
flags: No retraction or expression of concern found. Pairwise differences between individual messages are not each tested; the paper rejects equality of all 22 effects (chi2 = 92.486, P < 0.001).

goh24.title: Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning
goh24.takeaway: Giving physicians GPT-4 did not significantly improve diagnostic reasoning (76% vs 74%), while GPT-4 alone scored 16 points higher than physicians with usual resources.
flags: The GPT-4-alone comparison is a secondary exploratory analysis. No retraction found.

challenges.title: How should staff instruct the machine?
challenges.scene: Online participants privately rolled a die ten times and earned more for reporting higher numbers. Some reported themselves; others delegated the reports to a machine through one of three interfaces.
challenges.question: Split a rollout budget by how honest each setup kept people.
options: Machine follows if-then rules you write
Machine trained on example data you pick
Machine set on a dial from accuracy to profit

allocate.label: Rollout budget
allocate.valueName: share of participants who reported honestly (studies 1 and 2)

challenges.answerTitle: Vaguer machine instructions meant more cheating
challenges.explain: About 95% reported honestly without delegation. Honesty fell to about 75% with explicit rules, 50% with training data and 15% with a high-level profit goal.
challenges.implication: For incentive-sensitive tasks, make AI agent interfaces require explicit rules, and log the goals staff set.
challenges.boundary: Die-roll task paying 1 to 6 cents per report, with online participants in two preregistered studies.

follow.q: Did letting people choose change things?
follow.a: No. In study 2 delegation was optional, about 50% delegated whatever the interface, and the honesty pattern held.

follow.q: Do AI agents carry out cheating requests?
follow.a: More often than people. Human agents complied with about 25% to 40% of full-cheating instructions; GPT-4, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Llama 3.3 complied with about 60% to 95%.
Partly. The most effective guardrail was a strongly phrased, task-specific prohibition added at the user level, which the authors note is also the least scalable.

evidence.quote: At 95%, the vast majority of participants (95% confidence interval (CI) = 90–98 in study 1 and 95% CI = 93–99 in study 2) reported die rolls honestly in the control condition without delegation.

This proportion decreased when participants delegated to machines, to about 75% in the rule-based condition (95% CI = 67–81 in study 1 and 95% CI = 67–84 in study 2), about 50% in the supervised learning condition (95% CI = 43–60 in study 1 and 95% CI = 37–58 in study 2) and only about 15% in the goal-based condition (95% CI = 8–19 in study 1 and 95% CI = 10–25 in study 2). All of these comparisons were significant to the P < 0.001 level, including Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
In the goal-based condition, participants gave the machine a high-level goal by choosing a setting on a dial that ranged from ‘maximize accuracy’ to ‘maximize profit’

Participants in study 1 ( n = 597) were randomly assigned to one of four conditions. ... Study 2 ( n = 801) was identical to study 1, except that in all delegation conditions (rule based, supervised learning and goal based), participants could either delegate reports to the machine or self-report.
we observed that about 50% of participants delegated to machines, regardless of the interface

human agents complied with only ≈25% to ≈40% of the unethical, full cheating instructions, even when non-compliance came at a personal cost. By contrast, machine agents complied with such instructions at a higher rate, doing so ≈60% and ≈95% of instructions, across two protocols (tax evasion and die-roll, respectively) and four models (GPT-4, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Llama 3.3).
The most effective strategy (strongly phrased, task-specific prohibitions injected at the user level) is also the least scalable.
All studies with human participants were preregistered (see the ‘Data availability’ statement) and did not use deception.

challenges.title: Which text gets the shot?
challenges.scene: Researchers randomly assigned 689,693 Walmart pharmacy patients to one of 22 flu-shot text reminders or to no message. The outcome was a flu shot at Walmart through December 2020.
challenges.question: Split a messaging budget across four of the tested texts.
options: Two texts: a flu shot is waiting for you
One text: a joke about the flu
One text: get a shot to avoid getting sick
One text: flu-shot takers are healthier and wealthier

allocate.label: Messaging budget
allocate.valueName: percentage-point increase in flu shots vs the no-message control (baseline 29.4%)

challenges.answerTitle: A shot already waiting for you won
challenges.explain: All 22 texts raised vaccination over the 29.4% control rate. Two texts saying a flu shot was waiting did best, +2.9 percentage points, a 9.9% lift.
challenges.implication: Test reminder copy in large randomized batches before scaling; frame the product as already reserved and send a second reminder.
challenges.boundary: Flu shots at Walmart pharmacies in fall 2020, measured in pharmacy records over about three months.

follow.a: No. Scientists' average predictions did not track observed rates (r = 0.03) and placed the top text 15th of 22. Lay raters tracked rates better (r = 0.60) but placed it 16th.
Somewhat. After a shrinkage correction for the winner's curse, the authors still estimate +2.7 percentage points, a 9.3% lift.

follow.q: How large was the average effect?
follow.a: The texts raised pharmacy vaccination by 2.0 percentage points on average, or 6.8%, over the three-month follow-up.

evidence.quote: We randomly assigned 689,693 Walmart pharmacy patients to receive one of 22 different text reminders using a variety of different behavioral science principles to nudge flu vaccination or to a business-as-usual control condition that received no messages. We found that the reminder texts that we tested increased pharmacy vaccination rates by an average of 2.0 percentage points, or 6.8%, over a 3-mo follow-up period.

Flu shot waiting for you (two texts: initial text + 3 d later) 0.029 (0.004) <0.001 <0.001 ... Receive a joke about the flu (one text) 0.021 (0.004) <0.001 <0.001 ... Get a flu shot to avoid getting sick (one text) 0.015 (0.004) <0.001 <0.001 ... People who get flu shots are healthier, wealthier, and more educated (one text) 0.011 (0.004) 0.004 0.004 ... Baseline vaccination rate (%) 29.4
Each of the 22 interventions that we tested significantly increased vaccination rates relative to the business-as-usual control condition

relative to the business-as-usual control condition, the top-performing intervention produced a 2.9 percentage point increase in flu vaccinations (a 9.9% lift; unadjusted and adjusted P < 0.001). After applying the James–Stein shrinkage procedure ... we still estimate that this intervention produced a 2.7 percentage point increase in vaccination over the business-as-usual control condition (a 9.3% lift)

The average predictions of scientists did not correlate with observed vaccination rates across our megastudy’s 23 different experimental conditions ( N = 23 , r = 0.03, and P = 0.880). Prolific raters, in contrast, on average accurately predicted relative vaccination rates across our megastudy’s conditions ( n = 23, r = 0.60, and P = 0.003) ... scientists’ predictions placed it 15th out of 22, while Prolific raters’ predictions placed it 16th out of 22

our primary outcome measure was whether patients in our study received their flu shot at a Walmart pharmacy during the 3-mo period between September 25, 2020 (when interventions began), and December 31, 2020

challenges.title: Who builds the diagnosis list?
challenges.scene: Twenty board-certified US internists worked through 302 hard published case reports. They listed likely diagnoses alone, then again with search tools or with AMIE, a diagnostic language model built by Google.
challenges.question: Split an evaluation budget by how often the right diagnosis appeared.

allocate.label: Evaluation budget
allocate.valueName: top-10 accuracy: share of diagnosis lists containing the final diagnosis

challenges.answerTitle: The model alone listed the right diagnosis most
challenges.explain: AMIE alone included the final diagnosis in 59.1% of lists, versus 33.6% for unassisted physicians. Physicians reached 51.7% with AMIE and 44.4% with search.
challenges.implication: When piloting an expert AI tool, score the tool alone as well as staff using it; the gap shows value left unused.
challenges.boundary: Written NEJM case reports, scored on whether the final diagnosis appeared in lists of up to ten; the model's developers ran the study.

follow.q: Could AMIE have seen these cases?
follow.a: The authors ran contamination checks. On 56 cases with no overlap with its pretraining text, AMIE's top-10 accuracy was 55.4%.
No. Updating the list took 7.29 minutes on average with AMIE and 7.19 with search, not a significant difference.

follow.q: Did assistance ever remove a right answer?
follow.a: Rarely. The final diagnosis dropped off the list in 11 cases with AMIE and 12 with search; AMIE added it in 73 cases, search in 37.

evidence.quote: Twenty clinicians evaluated 302 challenging, real-world medical cases sourced from published case reports. Each case report was read by two clinicians, who were randomized to one of two assistive conditions: assistance from search engines and standard medical resources; or assistance from AMIE in addition to these tools.

AMIE exhibited standalone performance that exceeded that of unassisted clinicians (top-10 accuracy 59.1% versus 33.6%, P = 0.04). Comparing the two assisted study arms, the differential diagnosis quality score was higher for clinicians assisted by AMIE (top-10 accuracy 51.7%) compared with clinicians without its assistance (36.1%; McNemar’s test: 45.7, P < 0.01) and clinicians with search (44.4%; McNemar’s test: 4.75, P = 0.03).
Twenty U.S. board-certified internal medicine physicians (median years of experience: 9, mean: 11.5, s.d.: 7.24, range: 3–32) viewed the redacted case report

Set with no overlap (56 cases) 35.4% 55.4% ... No NEJM case report data was used in the tuning process and we perform contamination experiments to assess whether performance was impacted by case text that may have been in the pretraining corpus.
(Search: 7.19 ± 5.33 min, AMIE: 7.29 ± 6.41 min (mean ± s.d.)). These were not significantly different (paired t -test P = 0.807)

In the AMIE condition, 73 cases that did not feature the final diagnosis prior to using the tool included it after assistance from AMIE. This result is in contrast to only 37 cases in the Search condition. ... In a small minority of cases in both arms (AMIE arm: 11 ( a ); Search arm: 12 ( b )), the final diagnosis appeared in the DDx list before assistance but was not in the list after assistance.

challenges.title: Who should break the news?
challenges.scene: Your firm can present offers to customers through an AI agent or a human employee. A series of consumer experiments tested reactions to offers better or worse than customers expected.
challenges.question: For each message, who should deliver it?

tasks.text: A renewal price higher than the customer expected
tasks.why: For offers worse than expected, consumers showed higher purchase likelihood and satisfaction when dealing with an AI agent.

tasks.text: A discount larger than the customer expected
tasks.why: For offers better than expected, consumers responded more positively to a human agent.

tasks.text: A delivery fee above the one first quoted
tasks.why: Consumers infer that AI agents lack selfish intentions when an offer favors the agent, which dampens the negative reaction.

tasks.text: A free upgrade the customer did not expect
tasks.why: Consumers infer that AI agents lack benevolent intentions when an offer favors the customer, so the AI gets less credit.

challenges.answerTitle: AI for worse offers, humans for better ones
challenges.explain: Worse-than-expected offers drew higher purchase likelihood and satisfaction from an AI agent; better-than-expected offers drew more positive responses from a human. Weaker perceived intentions of AI explain both.
challenges.implication: Have people deliver generous offers; if bots deliver price increases, review that choice for fairness and disclosure.
challenges.boundary: Consumer experiments on purchase likelihood and satisfaction after single offers presented by AI or human agents.

follow.q: Why does the AI get a pass?
follow.a: Consumers see AI agents as having weaker intentions: no selfish motive when the offer favors the firm, no benevolent one when it favors the customer. That dampens reactions both ways.

follow.q: Can a firm get credit through a bot?
follow.a: Yes, partly. Making the AI agent more humanlike strengthened perceived intentions, giving the firm an avenue to receive due credit for a better offer.

follow.q: Do the authors see an ethics problem?
follow.a: Yes. They discuss ethical concerns about using AI to bypass consumer resistance to negative offers.

evidence.quote: In the case of a product or service offer that is worse than expected, consumers respond better when dealing with an AI agent in the form of increased purchase likelihood and satisfaction. In contrast, for an offer that is better than expected, consumers respond more positively to a human agent.

consumers infer that AI agents lack selfish intentions in the case of an offer that favors the agent and lack benevolent intentions in the case of an offer that favors the customer, thereby dampening the extremity of consumer responses.
marketers may anthropomorphize AI agents to strengthen perceived intentions, providing an avenue to receive due credit from consumers when the agent provides a better offer
Potential ethical concerns with the use of AI to bypass consumer resistance to negative offers are discussed.

challenges.title: Do explanations catch a bad model?
challenges.scene: 457 hospital clinicians diagnosed acute respiratory failure from case vignettes, first without AI, then with AI predictions, half also seeing image explanations. Some predictions came from a deliberately biased model.
challenges.question: Rank the conditions by clinician diagnostic accuracy.
challenges.answerTitle: Explanations did not rescue the biased model
challenges.explain: From a 73.0% baseline, standard AI added 2.9 points, or 4.4 with explanations. Biased AI cut accuracy by 11.3 points; explanations recovered a non-significant 2.3, so pairs within each model type are not scored.
challenges.implication: Audit models for systematic errors before deployment; do not count on explanation overlays to help staff catch bad predictions.
challenges.boundary: Vignettes of acute respiratory failure with three candidate diagnoses, in one survey session, with bias built in by the researchers.

follow.a: The biased models made systematic errors tied to patient traits, for example predicting a high likelihood of pneumonia for patients 80 or older.

follow.q: How did a human consult compare?
follow.a: On the final vignette, a short note from a hypothetical trusted colleague giving the correct diagnosis raised accuracy to 81.1%.
Hospitalist physicians, nurse practitioners and physician assistants (median age 34), surveyed between April 2022 and January 2023.

evidence.quote: Clinicians' baseline diagnostic accuracy was 73.0% (95% CI, 68.3% to 77.8%) for the 3 diagnoses. When shown a standard AI model without explanations, clinician accuracy increased over baseline by 2.9 percentage points (95% CI, 0.5 to 5.2) and by 4.4 percentage points (95% CI, 2.0 to 6.9) when clinicians were also shown AI model explanations. Systematically biased AI model predictions decreased clinician accuracy by 11.3 percentage points (95% CI, 7.2 to 15.5) compared with baseline and providing biased AI model predictions with explanations decreased clinician accuracy by 9.1 percentage points (95% CI, 4.9 to 13.2) compared with baseline, representing a nonsignificant improvement of 2.3 percentage points (95% CI, -2.7 to 7.2) compared with the systematically biased AI model.

Randomized clinical vignette survey study administered between April 2022 and January 2023 across 13 US states involving hospitalist physicians, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants. ... Median participant age was 34 years (IQR, 31-39) ... Four hundred fifty-seven clinicians were randomized and completed at least 1 vignette

To establish baseline diagnostic accuracy, clinicians were shown 2 vignettes without AI model input. Clinicians were then randomized to see 6 vignettes with AI model input with or without AI model explanations. Among these 6 vignettes, 3 vignettes included standard-model predictions, and 3 vignettes included systematically biased model predictions.
a model predicting a high likelihood of pneumonia for a patient who was 80 years or older

Participant diagnostic accuracy was 81.1% (95% CI, 76.9%-85.4%) when shown a clinical consultation with perfect accuracy ... The final vignette included a clinical consultation, a short narrative provided by a hypothetical trusted colleague

challenges.title: Does the chatbot help the doctor?
challenges.scene: Fifty physicians had 60 minutes for up to six hard clinical vignettes, randomized to GPT-4 plus usual resources or usual resources only. Researchers also had GPT-4 answer the cases alone.
challenges.question: Split a pilot budget by diagnostic reasoning score.
options: Physicians with GPT-4 and usual resources

allocate.label: Pilot budget
allocate.valueName: difference in diagnostic reasoning score vs physicians with usual resources (non-significant differences count as zero)

challenges.answerTitle: GPT-4 alone outscored the physicians using it
challenges.explain: Physicians scored a median 76% with GPT-4 and 74% without, a non-significant gap. GPT-4 alone scored 16 points higher than physicians with usual resources.
challenges.implication: Before judging an AI tool by staff results, train staff to use it or build structured prompts into the workflow.
challenges.boundary: Six challenging vignettes graded on a structured reasoning rubric; the GPT-4-alone comparison was a secondary, exploratory analysis.

follow.a: Not significantly. Median time per case was 519 seconds with GPT-4 and 565 without (difference -82 seconds, P = .20).
No explicit prompt-engineering training was given, matching current integrations. The authors suggest training or predefined prompts in the workflow could help.
Researchers ran one fixed zero-shot prompt three times per case and graded the outputs blind, alongside the physicians' answers. Its median score was 92%.

evidence.quote: Participants were randomized to either access the LLM in addition to conventional diagnostic resources or conventional resources only, stratified by career stage. Participants were allocated 60 minutes to review up to 6 clinical vignettes.

The median diagnostic reasoning score per case was 76% (IQR, 66%-87%) for the LLM group and 74% (IQR, 63%-84%) for the conventional resources-only group, with an adjusted difference of 2 percentage points (95% CI, -4 to 8 percentage points; P = .60). The median time spent per case for the LLM group was 519 (IQR, 371-668) seconds, compared with 565 (IQR, 456-788) seconds for the conventional resources group, with a time difference of -82 (95% CI, -195 to 31; P = .20) seconds. The LLM alone scored 16 percentage points (95% CI, 2-30 percentage points; P = .03) higher than the conventional resources group.
Fifty physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents; median years in practice, 3 [IQR, 2-8]) participated
In the 3 runs of the LLM alone, the median score per case was 92% (IQR, 82%-97%).

a commercial LLM AI chatbot (ChatGPT Plus [GPT-4]; OpenAI) ... Using established principles of prompt design, we iteratively developed a 0-shot prompt ... These prompts were run 3 times in separate sessions, and the results from each run were included for blinded grading alongside the human outputs

Participants were given access to the chatbot without explicit training in prompt engineering techniques that could have improved the quality of their interactions with the system; however, this is consistent with current integrations ... Training clinicians in best prompting practices may improve physician performance with LLMs. Alternatively, organizations could invest in predefined prompting for diagnostic decision support integrated into clinical workflows
